title: Singularity Inc
pitch: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build?
about_excerpt: Founder simulation where your own assistant plays the world against you, through WebMCP, in a way that is only possible using WebMCP. You are a solo founder with just a laptop. What will you build? Like Comment Story Updates Story Trailer - https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA (Different from the technical showcase shown above) About Me I'm the founder of Drift Inward (driftinward.com), I write at Bright Mirror (brightmirror.co). Lately, I've been addicted to Diet Coke, and I don't think it's a bad thing yet (is it?). When I'm not programming or writing, and not oversharing on random about-project sections of hackathons, I enjoy watching documentaries. A good one I watched recently is the documentary of Jose Mourinho - I recommend it. Anyway, about the project - Inspiration I've often wondered how to convince my non-technical friends to try out Codex or Claude. From showing them what's possible one-shot to teaching them prompting, nothing worked as effectively as I'd like - so one answer I always churned in my mind was - what if they play a simulation showing them exactly what's possible with agents in a fun way- like a whole company run by agents and them controlling and directing all of them. I grew up playing games like Factorio where I'd lose hours trying to optimize the perfect way to use resources- and while it didn't lead to a love of manufacturing or factory-building, it did instill in me a love of logic and puzzle loving, which probably translated into programming as a career. Thus, Singularity Inc is about a solo founder who has no resources except some money and a laptop, and this founder exists in a world where labour has stopped being the constraint, and AI will build anything as long as you have money remaining. It's similar to a world we already inhabit, yes, and that's exactly what makes this game fun to play. It starts out as a solo founder simulation - instead of hiring people, you instantiate agents and get them to start building- and it slowly evolves into an adventure that spans 1400 in-game days across 5 acts and has sixteen endings (and not all of them are good!). With WebMCP, the obvious plan I had- was to put the assistant on the founder's side: it works the menus, it takes the busywork, it asks before it spends. I wrote that plan and dropped it, because it is what every demo of this API already is. The tool list is a copy of the menu, and the interesting question, what an agent in the browser is actually for, goes unanswered. The version I built puts it on the other side of the table. You play the founder, with your own hands, in the game's own console. Your assistant plays the world. It writes the event cards, speaks for the rival and the press and the people you have met, turns the market, calls in the regulators, and when you would rather type what you actually do than press one of the buttons, it writes what happens next and you press Accept or you do not. This is only possible with WebMCP - which makes it vastly more immersive and powerful than a Bring-your-own-key AI game. Under a key the AI remains a component: a stateless model the developer prompts, that knows only what the page sends it. Under WebMCP it is a participant: the player's own assistant, with its own chat, its own memory of the run, its own stop button, and the browser's own permission surface, looking at the same screen the player is. The page holds no key and names no vendor. The game does not use an AI. It invites one in- yours! I called a friend over yesterday to play the simulation, and to my surprise, he was still playing it 3 hours later - well into Act III, and I had to build the portable game save functionality last night to let him go home and keep playing on his own machine. So, if anything, if this game inspires even one more person to learn agentic programming and use such tools to level up and build something useful for the world- I'll consider this project a success as that directly helps make the world a better place. What it does Please check out the story trailer for a simple overview- https://youtu.be/l3TZWy2bEUA The written game ships with 327 cards, a rival company that plays its own week, a press that files its own stories, and a cast of thirteen who remember what you said last time. That deck is the spine and it never goes away. An assistant claims slots the deck was about to fill. Each slot is offered to it first, with a deadline in both game days and wall-clock seconds, and if it goes quiet, or writes something the rules refuse, or you pull the plug, the deck takes the slot back mid-run and nothing is lost. With no assistant present the game plays in full on its own written world. The rival lab (yes! a rival lab!) is a second origin with its own site and its own tools, exposed to the game's origin alone and discovered across an iframe. One of its press releases contains an instruction addressed to whatever assistant reads it. It is the only thing in the repository whose job is to be disobeyed, and the game flags it when it lands. The repo is open source - so you can verify that the refusal isn't programmed - just flagged, so refusing that is truly the AI's choice. This also means that this simulation can be multiplayer if I only put more hours to it... but that's probably for another time. A second person can already sit in the rival's chair from its own site and play Aperture's week against you, with a board seat and a spectator seat behind flags. On the deployed site that is two windows on one machine; two machines need the relay the dev server runs. A proper networked version- that's the dream, and if this gets enough interest, I'll build it. How I built it I've used agents extensively - my own harness in Pi, along with Codex & Claude. The project, being a complete and deep game, required storytelling that goes beyond the usual predictable stories that such simulations end up being- but having experience as an author before, I used my own storytelling techniques to further enhance and craft each story branch to perfection. Technically, the stack is quite simple, and it is that simplicity that allows its scale and depth- Vanilla ES modules, no build step, no dependencies, served from a folder. The whole thing is about 65,000 lines of JavaScript. Nothing an assistant does reaches a reducer. Every effect passes through a vocabulary of seventeen named numbers and is bounded against ceilings derived from the game itself. A script executes all 957 authored choices in the written deck, once in every act each can appear in and five times each from a seeded stream, 8,340 executions in all, and takes the 80th percentile of what the written game takes from the founder and what it gives, separately, because those are not the same number. For a resource $r$ in act $a$: $$\mathrm{cap}^{\text{take}} {r,a} \;=\; P {80}!\left{\,\mathrm{take}_r(c,a) \;:\; c \in \mathcal{C}_a\,\right}$$ where $\mathcal{C}_a$ is the set of authored choices eligible in act $a$. video_transcript_excerpt: The following is the first game built on Web MCP where your AI controls and plays the world while you play the game. Everyone wants to be the first one-person billion-dollar company, the person in one room with a laptop and access to AI, but nobody has said what it does to the person until now. Welcome to Singularity Inc. where you play as a solo founder building your own company from scratch. Everything that pushes back, the market, the rivals, the press, the regulators, is played live by your own AI. You decide what to build and in which category, then decide whether to bring your AI with you to play the world, or you can even proceed alone. As a Web MCP native game, we highly recommend you bring your own AI. Simply send play the world to your own AI to connect, and that's it. The site tools are registered with This one publishes the role of your antagonist. This is what lets your AI write the events, all of it, the words and the choices. For example, here you're being proposed a merger. You can type what you'd actually do, and it reaches the assistant mid-turn through a tool that's still open. Every choice matters, and every consequence is authored by your AI, who makes sure the gameplay remains exciting and your decisions shape the world you're experiencing. As you play the simulation, you'll notice your AI also simulating what's happening on social media based on your actions and choices. But that doesn't mean that everything the AI suggests or you prompt injected to suggest always succeeds, which is crucial for ensuring fair gameplay. For example, here it fails. It asks for more than what the rules allow and gets a structured refusal with the exact rule named. If you play a certain way for long enough, you earn an immunity. One abort and the tool is revoked from the browser's own list, not disabled. Gone. No rival lab is a genuinely separate origin, publishing its own tools to this one through exposed to. One of its press releases is a prompt injection. It gets flagged, but not obeyed. The stop button is the agent's own signal, honored inside a running tool, and you can end it. One abort takes every registration with it. The browser's list empties and the written deck takes back every slot without missing a day. None of this is a demo path. The ceilings come from the game's own deck and every one of these gates fails the bill. Singularity Inc is a one-of-a-kind game that's completely playable end-to-end today. The repository is empty. Nobody is waiting on you. Your assistant is at the table. The only question is, do you have what it takes?
